slides.title: Nook
slides.purpose: Introduce the project and team.
slides.key_message: A student community with collaborative coding competition.
slide_content: Community and competitive coding
ft_transcendence
sel-mlil, ayousr, amsbai, elakhfif
slides.speaker_notes: Nook brings a student community and competitive coding into the same application. We will follow a user through the product, explain the service boundaries, and show the engineering behind identity, messaging and Code Arena. The technical review closes with the evidence we have and the checks still required for evaluation.
technical_details: The product combines a feed, people discovery, direct conversations, groups and Code Arena.
The presentation uses the repository state reviewed on 2026-11-15.

slides.title: A community built around participation
slides.purpose: Explain the product purpose and implemented scope.
slides.key_message: Students can share work, connect with peers and compete through one account.
slide_content: Feed: posts with text and media.
People: profiles, search and friendships.
Chat: direct conversations and group channels.
Play: Code Arena duels and team matches.
slides.speaker_notes: The four spaces serve one journey. A student can discover someone through a post or search, open their profile, start a conversation and challenge them to a coding match. The current feed is global. A following-based feed remains product direction, rather than implemented behavior. Code Arena is the playable game; Chess is a coming-soon route.
technical_details: Feed reuses the Chat Message model.
Profile actions bridge User, Chat and Game through APIs.
App-shell notifications are sample data and several settings sections remain marked Soon.

slides.title: The team and its responsibilities
slides.purpose: State documented contribution boundaries.
slides.key_message: Product, application and game work meet at shared integration decisions.
slide_content: sel-mlil: product ownership, technical direction, User management and Chat integration.
ayousr: project coordination, Game service, Judge server and 2v2 integration.
amsbai: Chat planning and 1v1 design contributions.
elakhfif: infrastructure guidance, Nginx and Grafana specifications.
slides.speaker_notes: These responsibilities follow the team contribution table in the README. Sel-mlil proposed the project and selected its stack, built User management and its Next.js integration, implemented Chat endpoints and client integration, and co-developed infrastructure specifications with elakhfif. Ayousr coordinated work through Trello and Discord and built the game service and judge server. Amsbai helped plan Chat and contributed to 1v1 decisions. Elakhfif contributed infrastructure guidance. Sel-mlil also created FT Trans Score for module and evidence tracking.
technical_details: Attribution comes from the team-maintained README, not an inference from file ownership or commit counts.
Presenter assignments in this deck are suggestions for rehearsal.

slides.title: One identity across the user journey
slides.purpose: Connect product surfaces before introducing service details.
slides.key_message: The profile connects social activity to conversations and matches.
slide_content: Find a student through search or a post.
Open a profile and manage a friendship.
Start a conversation or invite them to Code Arena.
slides.speaker_notes: Use the profile screenshot to anchor the architecture in something visible. The profile belongs to the User domain, the Message action opens Chat, and the challenge action creates a Game room. Those actions share the same account UUID while each service retains responsibility for its own data.
technical_details: User UUIDs act as shared identifiers.
Chat stores a public-profile projection with the original User UUID.
Game validates the JWT subject and resolves display details through User APIs.

slides.title: System architecture
slides.purpose: Show browser routing, domain services and data ownership.
slides.key_message: Nginx routes the client to services with separate responsibilities and databases.
slide_content: User owns identity. Chat owns conversations. Game owns competition.
RabbitMQ carries service events. Socket.IO carries client updates.
Game delegates code execution to a private Judge worker.
slides.speaker_notes: Read the diagram from the browser downwards. Nginx routes web pages to Next.js and API paths to User, Chat and Game. Each application service owns a PostgreSQL database. RabbitMQ distributes profile changes and account deletion, and also Game lifecycle notices to Chat. Chat stores attachments in MinIO. Game calls the Judge worker across a private network. The Judge worker is a Node HTTP service; do not describe it as a NestJS application simply because the README stack summary groups the backends together.
technical_details: User and Chat use Prisma. Game uses parameterized SQL and durable match snapshots.
No cross-database foreign keys or direct cross-service database reads.
The Judge worker uses node:http in services/judge-worker/src/http-server.ts.
Initial Game deployment uses one instance under ADR-0016.
slides.visual_suggestion: Editable service and database diagram with routed connections.

slides.title: Technology choices and their trade-offs
slides.purpose: Explain the stack through project needs.
slides.key_message: A shared TypeScript stack supports the application, with specialist tools for data and collaboration.
slide_content: Next.js and React support routing, server-rendered pages and interactive views.
NestJS structures User, Chat and Game APIs.
PostgreSQL provides relational persistence.
Socket.IO, RabbitMQ and Yjs solve different communication problems.
slides.speaker_notes: Present the reasons as technical fit, rather than claiming every trade-off was explicitly documented at project kickoff. Next.js provides the route shell and server-rendered surfaces. NestJS offers modules, dependency injection, guards and DTO validation. PostgreSQL fits account relationships and durable game records. Socket.IO delivers live events, RabbitMQ decouples service updates, and Yjs merges concurrent editor changes. This architecture increases the amount of configuration and integration work compared with a single service.
technical_details: Prisma handles User/Chat models and migrations.
Game keeps explicit SQL persistence for match snapshots and atomic state changes.
A browser editor needs client-only rendering and dynamic loading.
Multiple services require coordinated contracts, configuration and operational visibility.
slides.visual_suggestion: Native editable reference table.

slides.title: Data belongs to a service
slides.purpose: Explain persistence and boundaries.
slides.key_message: Shared user identifiers connect the domains without sharing database ownership.
slide_content: User: credentials, sessions, profiles and social relationships.
Chat: conversations, membership, messages and read markers.
Game: rooms, snapshots, submissions and results.
MinIO: attachment bytes referenced by object keys.
slides.speaker_notes: Separate databases make ownership visible. ChatUser is a local projection, not a second credential store. An attachment message stores an object key, not a signed URL that will expire. Game keeps durable state for restart and recovery, but live socket fan-out still requires the chosen deployment topology. There is no single transaction spanning the three databases.
technical_details: UserImage stores profile image data in User PostgreSQL.
Message.attachments stores MinIO object keys.
Game stores match and collaborative document snapshots.
Cross-service consistency relies on explicit APIs and events.
table: Rooms, match snapshots, rounds, submissions, editor state
slides.visual_suggestion: Native editable reference table.

slides.title: Frontend structure and session-aware data
slides.purpose: Explain how the client organizes routes and server state.
slides.key_message: Typed API clients and shared session handling connect the interface to the services.
slide_content: App Router groups separate public, authentication and application layouts.
Typed clients call same-origin /api paths.
TanStack Query manages server state and message history.
Nook tokens keep shared components visually consistent.
slides.speaker_notes: The client uses Next.js 16, React 19 and Tailwind CSS 4. AuthProvider centralizes session state and requestWithSession. Access tokens stay in memory. Concurrent refreshes share one promise so rotating refresh tokens are not accidentally reused. Socket events merge messages into the query cache, and polling fills gaps. The application follows light, dark and system themes. The code editor loads as a client component because it needs browser APIs.
technical_details: API helpers live in client/lib/auth, accounts, social and chat.
Chat infinite-query keys include viewer and conversation identifiers.
HTTP responses and socket events deduplicate by id or clientRequestId.
The app shell reads sidebar_state under Suspense.
The design token source is client/NOOK_DESIGN_SYSTEM.json.
slides.visual_suggestion: Flat editorial composition with large numbered technical points.

slides.title: Authentication and session renewal
slides.purpose: Show the trust boundary and token lifecycle.
slides.key_message: User signs access tokens. Other services verify them with the public key.
slide_content: Login returns a 15-minute RS256 access token.
A 7-day refresh token lives in an HttpOnly cookie.
Refreshing rotates the token and restores the in-memory session.
Chat and Game verify signature, claims and account identity.
slides.speaker_notes: Credentials belong only to User. Password registration uses bcrypt with cost 12. The access JWT has issuer user-service and audience ft-transcendence-api, with a UUID subject. A page reload clears the in-memory access token, so the browser restores the session through the refresh cookie. Reusing an unexpired revoked refresh token revokes that login session. Logging out revokes refresh tokens, while already issued access tokens remain valid until expiry unless a separate service-specific revocation rule applies.
technical_details: The signing private key belongs only to User.
Chat and Game receive the matching public key.
Refresh requests share a promise in AuthProvider.
Nginx rewrites cookie path /auth/ to /api/auth/.
Do not claim universal immediate JWT invalidation on logout.
slides.visual_suggestion: Editable token-flow diagram from User through the browser to API consumers.

slides.title: Accounts and social relationships
slides.purpose: Cover account features and authorization.
slides.key_message: User service owns the account lifecycle and social rules.
slide_content: Registration, login, recovery and email verification.
Discord and GitHub OAuth login and account linking.
Editable profiles, images, search and friendship requests.
Blocks and superadmin operations with server checks.
slides.speaker_notes: The backend validates request DTOs and checks account state. Password-reset and verification tokens are hashed, single use and expire after two hours. Account search includes filtering, sorting and pagination. Roles are USER and SUPERADMIN, and protected administration reads the current database role. The service prevents deleting or demoting the last superadmin through transactional locking. Two-factor models exist in the schema, but there are no corresponding routes, so 2FA is not part of the feature claim.
technical_details: Email changes clear emailVerifiedAt.
Login is possible before email verification under the current implementation.
Password reset revokes refresh tokens. Authenticated password changes have different current revocation behavior.
TwoFactorAuth and RecoveryCode are schema-only.
User profiles and social actions integrate into Next.js views.
slides.visual_suggestion: Flat editorial composition with large numbered technical points.

slides.title: Profile synchronization through RabbitMQ
slides.purpose: Explain asynchronous integration and delivery semantics.
slides.key_message: Chat keeps a local public profile projection and applies newer User events.
slide_content: User publishes to the durable user.events topic exchange.
chat.user-events binds to user.#.
Chat applies newer profile snapshots and acknowledges delivery.
The projection may lag while services or the broker recover.
slides.speaker_notes: User publishes user.created, user.updated and user.deleted envelopes. The envelope contains eventId, eventType, version, occurredAt and public profile data. The version is the source update timestamp. Chat uses a conditional update when the incoming timestamp is newer, then createMany with skipDuplicates for missing profiles. It acknowledges only after applying the event, and requeues on processing failure. This makes duplicate and older deliveries safe for the profile projection. Durable queues, persistent publication and publisher confirms improve delivery, but they do not make the User database write and publication one atomic transaction.
technical_details: Exchange user.events uses topic routing.
Messages are persistent and the publisher uses confirm channels.
Chat consumes manually with prefetch(1).
eventId is not stored for Chat profile deduplication. Timestamp ordering protects the projection.
Game receives user.deleted through its own durable queue.
Public snapshots exclude passwords, email and global role.
slides.visual_suggestion: Editable publish, broker and consume diagram.

slides.title: Chat delivery and safe retries
slides.purpose: Explain one concrete reliability mechanism.
slides.key_message: A logical message keeps one identity across retries, persistence and live delivery.
slide_content: The client creates a clientRequestId for each logical send.
The server hashes the payload. Changed reuse returns 409.
New messages save and broadcast once. Retries return the stored row.
Socket delivery and HTTP responses merge into the same cache entry.
slides.speaker_notes: A network timeout does not tell the browser whether the server saved a message. Reusing the same request identifier allows a safe retry. Chat stores requestHash with the author and clientRequestId. It saves and broadcasts a new message once, returns the same row for a matching retry, and rejects a mismatched retry. History uses createdAt and id as a stable order and a message UUID cursor. Read markers persist separately from transient typing events.
technical_details: Message content supports 1 to 2000 characters.
Message history limit is 1 to 100 with an extra row for has-more detection.
Only authors can edit or soft-delete their messages.
Soft deletion clears text and blocks future attachment-URL issuance.
Chat polls every 30 seconds with a socket and every 5 seconds without one, according to the client guide.
slides.visual_suggestion: Editable horizontal flow with supporting text.

slides.title: Groups and the global feed
slides.purpose: Show reuse and the boundaries of current functionality.
slides.key_message: The feed reuses Chat messaging while groups retain their own membership rules.
slide_content: Groups contain channels with per-group ADMIN or MEMBER roles.
A feed post is a Message in a reserved public group and channel.
Provisioning, backfill and account events keep feed membership current.
The current feed is global, requires text and has no likes or comments.
slides.speaker_notes: Reuse avoided a second implementation of pagination, attachments, safe retries and live delivery. FeedService provisions fixed group and channel identifiers idempotently. It backfills users in batches of 1000 and ensures membership on account events and lazy access. The reserved feed stays out of the normal group sidebar and cannot be managed like an ordinary group. This also creates limits: blocks do not filter global posts, edits and deletes appear on refetch, and fan-out scales with the number of users.
technical_details: Reaction exists in the schema but has no API.
There is no reply column for feed comments.
Only authors delete their posts. Feed-wide moderation is absent.
Global feed membership expands the presence audience at demo scale.
Groups use server authorization, not only hidden frontend controls.
slides.visual_suggestion: Two flat columns comparing the responsibilities.

slides.title: Private attachments with bounded access
slides.purpose: Explain the upload and download design.
slides.key_message: Chat authorizes access while the browser transfers bytes directly to MinIO.
slide_content: Chat issues a five-minute signed POST policy.
MinIO enforces key, content type and size constraints.
Chat checks the uploaded object before attaching it to a message.
Read access uses short-lived signed URLs after authorization.
slides.speaker_notes: The browser asks Chat for an upload policy, uploads the file to MinIO through the local TLS proxy, then sends its object key with the message. The key contains conversation and user identifiers plus a random UUID. Chat checks ownership, the object metadata and allowed limits. Images and PDFs have a 10 MiB limit; supported video has a 50 MiB limit, with at most five attachments per message. PostgreSQL stores keys rather than temporary URLs. Deleting a message stops new URLs, but previously issued URLs remain valid until expiry and orphaned objects remain stored.
technical_details: Uploads use presigned POST policy, not presigned PUT.
Downloads and previews use signed GET access.
The public signing endpoint and internal storage endpoint differ. Host preservation matters for the signature.
A signed URL is a bearer capability.
No malware scanning or immediate revocation of already-issued signed URLs is claimed.
slides.visual_suggestion: Editable horizontal flow with supporting text.

slides.title: Code Arena entry and matchmaking
slides.purpose: Introduce the game product through its actual interface.
slides.key_message: Players enter a duel or form teams through rooms, matchmaking and invitations.
slide_content: 1v1 matchmaking and private duels.
2v2 rooms for four participants.
Six-character private-room codes.
Invitations from profiles and direct conversations.
slides.speaker_notes: The Game service owns room membership and joinability. The invitation card polls a status such as Open, In Match or Expired, but the backend checks again when the user joins. Names and avatars come from the User API. The default pool selects three distinct seeded problem IDs, with a larger authored catalog deferred. Show the lobby or start a prepared match at this point if the live demonstration fits the schedule.
technical_details: Canonical routes include /play, /play/lobby/[code] and /play/match/[id].
The invitation status poll runs every ten seconds.
Profile and Chat invitations share Game-owned room rules.
Room ownership determines who may publish a challenge into a conversation.
slides.caption: Recorded Play screen
slides.visual_suggestion: Original project screenshot with editable explanatory text.

slides.title: Match rules and progression
slides.purpose: Explain server authority and the current gameplay transition.
slides.key_message: The server owns timing, scoring and the final outcome.
slide_content: Three distinct problems within a 30-minute match budget.
Run checks visible examples. Submit evaluates hidden tests.
Winner order: score, counted-submission time, counted submissions, then draw.
Current worktree: independent side progression and a final reveal.
slides.speaker_notes: The recorded November 14 match used shared round progression and per-round score reveals. ADR-0017 changes that flow: each player or team moves to its next problem after a counted evaluation or timeout, with a ten-minute per-problem cap clamped to the match budget. Opponents see progress but not scores or hidden-group results until the final reveal. The ADR says this is implemented on the feature branch with verification pending. Use the correct rules for the actual build being demonstrated.
technical_details: Current match phases are ROUND_INTRO, CODING, final SCORE_REVEAL and MATCH_COMPLETE.
Each side persists its problem index, stage and deadline.
A timeout without a counted score assigns zero for that problem.
Accepted evaluation work retains bounded grace.
Scoring and judging semantics are unchanged by the progression change.
slides.status_note: Independent progression is in the current worktree. Verification is pending.
slides.visual_suggestion: Flat editorial composition with large numbered technical points.

slides.title: 2v2 collaboration and readiness
slides.purpose: Explain concurrent editing and team rules.
slides.key_message: Teammates share a document and approve the revision they intend to submit.
slide_content: CodeMirror and Yjs merge concurrent edits.
Each team has its own document and match-scoped chat.
Readiness belongs to the current document revision.
A 90-second reconnect window governs teammate participation.
slides.speaker_notes: The team document is shared only inside the relevant team and match. Approvals apply to the document revision, so a returning teammate must approve the current revision again. An explicitly departed teammate, or one disconnected beyond the reconnect grace period, allows the remaining teammate to submit alone. Whole-team unavailability can end the match by forfeit. Team surrender requires agreement from the currently participating teammates. Yjs handles document convergence while the server owns access, readiness and submission rules.
technical_details: The Game /chat namespace is separate from the platform Chat service.
Team collaboration snapshots persist in Game storage.
One Game service instance is the initial release constraint.
Saved collaboration evidence shows teammate synchronization and separation from the opposing document.
slides.caption: Recorded 2v2 editor, before independent progression
slides.visual_suggestion: Original project screenshot with editable explanatory text.

slides.title: Judging untrusted code
slides.purpose: Explain isolation and resource admission.
slides.key_message: Game validates the submission and delegates execution to a constrained worker.
slide_content: Python, C++ and C use defined problem drivers.
A private worker endpoint requires a shared token.
A bounded queue controls concurrency and waiting work.
Execution containers disable networking and restrict resources.
slides.speaker_notes: The game checks the supported language and driver before dispatch. Python supports configured snippet entrypoints, while C and C++ use standard-input/output drivers. The worker has a bounded process queue, with defaults of two concurrent jobs and eight waiting jobs, subject to deployment settings. Container execution drops capabilities, disables networking, uses no-new-privileges, limits CPU, memory and process count, and makes the root filesystem read-only. The host Docker socket is mounted in the worker, so the worker is still a privileged host component.
technical_details: Default queue timeout is 30000 ms. Configuration can override the queue and concurrency defaults.
ContainerJudge compares outputs against the sealed suite.
Public history must not expose source code or hidden tests.
The worker uses Node HTTP, not NestJS.
Private network placement and a shared token do not remove Docker-host trust.
slides.visual_suggestion: Editable submission, queue, worker and sandbox pipeline.

slides.title: Persistent results and player progression
slides.purpose: Connect game records to long-term user features.
slides.key_message: Completed match records drive history, statistics and progression.
slide_content: History records opponents, dates, outcomes and scores.
XP awards 50 per match, plus 100 for a win or 25 for a draw.
Each 100 XP advances one level, starting at level 1.
Six achievements and a leaderboard expose progress.
slides.speaker_notes: Progression derives from durable completed records, so it is explainable. A win is 150 XP, a draw 75 and a loss 50 under the current rules. Level is floor(XP / 100) + 1. The winner can differ even when both sides have the same displayed score because time and counted submissions break ties. The leaderboard uses wins and win rate rather than an Elo system. The roadmap still asks the team to demonstrate statistics and progression across a service restart.
technical_details: Stats are calculated from completed match records.
Game owns match snapshots, round/submission records and collaborative state.
Public match summaries omit submitted code and hidden-test content.
Persistence in source does not by itself prove the live restart acceptance check.
slides.caption: Recorded profile Games tab
slides.visual_suggestion: Original project screenshot with editable explanatory text.

slides.title: Game events become conversation history
slides.purpose: Explain the Game-to-Chat integration.
slides.key_message: Chat persists lifecycle notices for the conversation that carries a challenge.
slide_content: Game authorizes the room owner before Chat binds an invitation.
Game publishes start, result and cancellation events.
Chat validates and persists one system notice per event.
Both clients receive the notice through Socket.IO.
slides.speaker_notes: An invitation and a lifecycle notification are separate behaviors. The invitation links a conversation to a Game room only after Game confirms the sender can announce it. Later Game publishes authoritative lifecycle events to game.events. Chat validates the participants and conversation, deduplicates delivery, and writes a SYSTEM message. Matchmaking games without a linked conversation do not produce platform Chat notices. The publisher has no durable outbox, so retries are best effort and a restart can lose in-flight publication.
technical_details: Game never writes to the Chat database.
GameChallenge records the conversation and room binding.
Notification payloads exclude source code and hidden tests.
November 11 evidence shows live invitation, start, result and cancellation notices in two sessions.
slides.caption: Recorded game-result notification in Chat
slides.visual_suggestion: Original project screenshot with editable explanatory text.

slides.title: Deployment and observability
slides.purpose: Explain how the system starts and how operators inspect it.
slides.key_message: Compose provides the service topology and Nginx provides the HTTPS entry point.
slide_content: Compose defines services, health checks, networks and persistent storage.
Nginx routes APIs, WebSockets, web pages and Grafana.
Prometheus collects metrics. Grafana displays dashboards and alerts.
Alloy and Loki support log collection and investigation.
slides.speaker_notes: The system runs as a multi-service Compose deployment. Most backend and database ports are private, while explicit development tools use loopback bindings. Local TLS is self-signed and requires local trust or acceptance. Prometheus, Loki and Alloy stay internal, with Grafana behind the gateway. Health checks and a status page help identify unavailable components. A healthy container does not prove that every user flow or recovery procedure works. The initial Game topology uses one instance because cross-instance coordination has not been validated.
technical_details: Environment templates describe ownership and required settings.
Node 22+ and Docker Compose support the documented setup and check scripts.
make up, make down and make check wrap common operations.
Logs should exclude secrets and signed URL capabilities.
Production DNS, OAuth callbacks and trusted TLS require target-environment configuration.
slides.visual_suggestion: Flat editorial composition with large numbered technical points.

slides.title: Recovery and account erasure
slides.purpose: Explain durable recovery and privacy effects across services.
slides.key_message: A complete recovery needs the databases and their associated attachment data.
slide_content: Complete snapshots include User, Chat, Game and MinIO.
Database-only backup containers are a separate optional profile.
Recovery must preserve the links between message rows and objects.
Account erasure anonymizes results and removes affected-side source data.
slides.speaker_notes: The complete snapshot workflow includes checksums and retention. Installing a host schedule is an operator step. The database-only profile can provide scheduled SQL backups, but it does not include MinIO. The three database dumps are individually consistent, rather than one cross-service atomic transaction. For erasure, Game receives user.deleted, removes lobby participation, ends affected active matches, anonymizes retained participant records and removes code and diagnostics for the affected side. Because 2v2 code belongs to a shared side, erasure removes that shared code too. Backups follow their separate retention policy.
technical_details: Do not claim an isolated clean-service restore merely from taking a snapshot.
Do not enable both backup schedules accidentally.
Deleted-account handling is event-driven and has documented propagation windows.
Historical credential exposure remains an operator action until rotation and revocation are confirmed.
slides.visual_suggestion: Two flat columns comparing the responsibilities.

slides.title: Recorded gameplay evidence
slides.purpose: Show the strongest saved demonstration with its scope.
slides.key_message: A recorded 2v2 run completed all three problems through evaluated submissions.
slide_content: 14 November: four browser clients completed three scored rounds.
Each side reached a total score of 300.
The run ended normally, without surrender or timeout.
All clients ran on one computer.
slides.speaker_notes: This is stronger evidence than the earlier collaboration-only run. The November 14 record describes passing evaluated submissions in all three rounds and normal match completion. The screenshot shows 300 against 300 and a win outcome. Equal displayed scores do not force a draw because the game also compares counted-submission time and then counted submissions. This evidence belongs to the previous shared-round flow and does not validate the new independent progression. Separate-computer play with disconnection recovery remains a different acceptance check.
technical_details: Evidence includes three per-round reveal screenshots and final completion.
Desktop, tablet and mobile images show the result modal fitting those viewports.
Those modal images do not prove every coding-workspace control is responsive.
The older roadmap paragraph only describes the November 12 run; the integration spec records the later run.
slides.caption: 14 November 2026, recorded 2v2 completion
slides.visual_suggestion: Original project screenshot with editable explanatory text.

slides.title: Module coverage and evaluation
slides.purpose: Summarize the README claim without equating it to an award.
slides.key_message: The README claims 22 modules and 31 raw points under the local tracker.
slide_content: Web: 10 modules, 12 raw points.
User: 4 modules, 6 raw points.
Game: 4 modules, 6 raw points.
DevOps: 3 modules, 5 raw points. Feed: 1 custom module, 2 raw points.
slides.speaker_notes: These totals are calculated from the README table, not awarded by staff. Nine major modules contribute 18 points and thirteen minor modules contribute 13. The local tracker has a 14-point required threshold and up to five bonus points. Mandatory foundation checks remain separate. U04 is excluded from the claim. The custom feed module requires evaluator acceptance. G03 appears in supporting gameplay evidence but is not in the README 22-module subtotal, so it is not silently added here.
technical_details: U01,U02,U03,U05 = 6 points.
G01,G02,G06,G09 = 6 points.
D02,D03,D04 = 5 points. C01 = 2 points.
Module labels are local tracker identifiers. The subject and evaluator govern acceptance.
slides.visual_suggestion: Large claim totals beside an editable module breakdown.

slides.title: Evaluation readiness
slides.purpose: Define a concrete rehearsal and readiness agenda.
slides.key_message: The next proof is a repeatable demonstration on the intended evaluation setup.
slide_content: Complete a match on separate computers and recover from a disconnection.
Demonstrate full Advanced Chat and persisted player statistics.
Perform fresh setup and isolated recovery with matching attachments.
Verify the independent-progression change before presenting it as settled.
slides.speaker_notes: Use this as the team rehearsal checklist. The project has recorded tests and demonstrations, but dated results do not certify the present worktree. The full project command is npm run check, which includes disposable database and broker integration suites. Full G06 requires showing blocking, invitations, lifecycle notifications, profile access, persistent history, typing and read receipts together. Deployment owners also need to close environment configuration and credential rotation actions before public production readiness can be claimed.
technical_details: The full gate records the checked commit and dirty worktree status.
No application tests or live flows were rerun while preparing this deck.
Source review and saved screenshots are reference evidence, not a fresh acceptance pass.
ADR-0017 explicitly records pending verification.
slides.visual_suggestion: Flat editorial composition with large numbered technical points.

slides.title: A complete flow to demonstrate
slides.purpose: Close with the product story and transition to live demo or questions.
slides.key_message: An account connects people, conversation and a persistent coding match.
slide_content: Sign in and open a profile.
Send a message and a game invitation.
Join the lobby and collaborate in the editor.
Complete a match and inspect its result and history.
slides.speaker_notes: Close the presentation by returning to the user journey. Each step has a clear service owner, and the integration makes the experience continuous. For a live demonstration, use prepared accounts, a known build and the correct gameplay rules. If time is short, show the account and invitation path live, then use the dated screenshots for the full match evidence. Open the appendix only when questions require deeper technical detail.
technical_details: Suggested main-deck time: approximately 25 minutes, plus demonstration and questions.
The following appendix slides provide routing, failure behavior, model relationships and source navigation.

slides.title: Appendix: request routing
slides.purpose: Provide an exact API routing reference.
slides.key_message: The gateway exposes canonical application paths and keeps service hostnames internal.
slide_content: User routes share the /api prefix.
Chat and Game use distinct HTTP and Socket.IO paths.
MinIO signed access uses a separate local TLS port.
slides.speaker_notes: Use this table to trace a browser request during questions. The more-specific Chat and Game routes take precedence over generic /api routing. Match, lobby, collaboration and team-chat namespaces use the Game transport path. A namespace is not the same thing as a Socket.IO transport URL. The local MinIO route uses port 9443 and is not the same origin as the application.
technical_details: Canonical User routes: /api/auth, /api/accounts and /api/social.
Canonical Chat transport: /api/chat/socket.io/.
Canonical Game transport: /api/game/socket.io/.
The local MinIO access path requires configured CORS and signature-compatible host forwarding.
slides.visual_suggestion: Native editable reference table.

slides.title: Appendix: failure behavior
slides.purpose: Prepare concrete answers to staff questions.
slides.key_message: Each failure path has a defined recovery mechanism and a known limit.
slide_content: Expired access token: refresh once with a shared in-flight request.
Ambiguous message send: retry the same request identifier.
Duplicate profile event: ignore older or equal source timestamps.
Lost Game notification: best-effort retry, with no durable outbox.
slides.speaker_notes: These cases distinguish operational reasoning from naming technologies. A transient HTTP failure preserves the browser session, while authoritative 401 responses clear it. A repeated message does not create a duplicate. RabbitMQ redelivery requires safe consumer behavior. A process restart can still lose an event that never reached a durable queue. One Game instance avoids claiming cross-instance socket coordination that the project has not established.
technical_details: HTTP 0/network failures and 5xx responses preserve the in-memory session.
Same message ID with a different payload returns 409.
Profile events use timestamp ordering, not an event-ID log.
Game process locks and live fan-out remain tied to one instance.
slides.visual_suggestion: Flat editorial composition with large numbered technical points.

slides.title: Appendix: domain relationships
slides.purpose: Provide a compact model reference for technical questions.
slides.key_message: Relational links stay inside the owning service database.
slide_content: User owns credentials, linked providers and social relationships.
Chat relates groups, conversations, messages and readers.
Game relates matches, sides, rounds and submissions.
Cross-service UUIDs represent identity without shared database constraints.
slides.speaker_notes: Explain the essential relationships, rather than every column. A User has provider and session records. Friendships and blocks relate two users. A Group has memberships and channel conversations. A Conversation has messages and per-user read state. A GameChallenge links an invitation conversation to a room. In Game, participants belong to sides and matches, with rounds, submissions and collaborative documents. The separate stores require application-level validation at the boundaries.
technical_details: A Conversation is DM or CHANNEL. DM IDs derive from a normalized pair of users.
GroupMember has a local group role.
Message stores authorId, clientRequestId, requestHash, kind and soft-delete state.
Game retains anonymized results while deleting affected-side source during erasure.
table: User has sessions/providers; users have friendships/blocks
Group has members/channels; Conversation has Messages
Match has sides/rounds/submissions and editor snapshots

likely_staff_questions.question: Why separate databases?
likely_staff_questions.answer: Each service controls its own schema and rules. APIs and events connect domains, with eventual consistency and operational complexity as trade-offs.

likely_staff_questions.question: Why both RabbitMQ and Socket.IO?
likely_staff_questions.answer: RabbitMQ moves events between services and buffers durable deliveries. Socket.IO pushes application updates to connected browser clients.

likely_staff_questions.question: How do you prevent duplicate messages?
likely_staff_questions.answer: A unique logical send identifier and request hash let Chat return the stored message for safe retries and reject mismatched payload reuse.

likely_staff_questions.question: Why a local ChatUser table?
likely_staff_questions.answer: Chat can join profile details to its own data without a synchronous User lookup for each render. Events update the public projection.

likely_staff_questions.question: What does Yjs solve?
likely_staff_questions.answer: It merges concurrent document changes. The server still enforces team access, revision approvals and submission rules.

likely_staff_questions.question: Does 300 against 300 mean a draw?
likely_staff_questions.answer: No. The winner order compares score, then total counted-submission time, then counted submissions, then draw.

likely_staff_questions.question: Can you scale Game horizontally now?
likely_staff_questions.answer: The initial release uses one instance under ADR-0016. Multi-instance coordination and fan-out need a separate design and verification.

likely_staff_questions.question: Is judging fully isolated from the host?
likely_staff_questions.answer: Execution containers have resource and network restrictions, but the worker mounts the host Docker socket and remains a privileged component.

likely_staff_questions.question: What is not implemented?
likely_staff_questions.answer: Chess, 2FA routes, feed likes/comments and several settings are not complete. The notification shell includes sample data. The full-project deck labels these limits.
